verdict.root_cause: At 01:34:26 UTC a platform-automation principal attached a traffic-shaping container to productcatalogservice's network namespace, applying a fixed 300 ms egress delay with zero jitter on eth0 (tr_a548b460d72d). Every caller that crosses the productcatalogservice boundary now pays that fixed penalty: caller-side spans from frontend, recommendationservice and checkoutservice cluster tightly at 301-308 ms while the matching server-side handler spans are ~0.0-0.1 ms, so the time is consumed on the wire between client send and handler entry, not inside the service (tr_0126c91be05d). The penalty stacks per call, so fan-out traces reach 612 ms, 1206-1526 ms and one checkout trace 3687 ms. Nothing is erroring — frontend and productcatalogservice error ratios are flat at zero across the whole window (tr_926489735ab4, tr_b4f2d77fccb8, tr_c1b38bb4b877) — so the incident is a latency-only degradation of the productcatalogservice call path, and the alerts on frontend, checkoutservice, recommendationservice and loadgenerator are the callers waiting on it. The failure mechanism is time spent waiting on a dependency, injected at the network layer; the change record is how it started, not the mechanism itself.
verdict.reasoning: Two independent lines converge. The change log gives a mechanism with the exact shape observed: a fixed 300 ms, zero-jitter egress delay installed roughly three minutes before onset (tr_a548b460d72d). The traces then confirm that shape empirically and localise it: durations are quantised into a narrow 301-308 ms band rather than heavy-tailed, the same floor appears for three distinct callers (so it is not a caller-side client or pool problem), the server-side spans are sub-millisecond with no children (so it is not the handler, a database, CPU saturation, or a downstream of productcatalogservice), and cart/currency/payment/shipping/email/quote spans in the same traces stay sub-millisecond to ~20 ms (so it is not cluster-wide) (tr_0126c91be05d). Three separate error-ratio queries are flat at zero with populated denominators, which rules out an error-rate event, a hard dependency failure, and a total outage, leaving slow-but-successful calls as the only surviving shape (tr_926489735ab4, tr_b4f2d77fccb8, tr_c1b38bb4b877). I classify this as dependency_latency rather than bad_config because the delay is not a wrong value being read by the service — it is time inserted into the call path, and the callers fail because they wait. Remediation is detaching the traffic-shaping container / reverting that automation action; a restart or rollback of productcatalogservice would not remove a delay installed in the network namespace, and scaling would not help a fixed per-call penalty. The retrieved product-catalog-flag-failure incident is a poor match for the primary signal: that one produced genuine errors from productcatalogservice's own code, and error ratios here are zero throughout.
open_questions: The second latency tier is unexplained: a minority of GetProduct calls run ~1207-1211 ms client-side with ~904-908 ms server-side, driven by a child FeatureFlagService/GetFlag call of essentially the same duration (tr_0126c91be05d). No dispatch examined FeatureFlagService. This is a distinct mechanism from the 300 ms step and may be a second concurrent fault, or a pre-existing condition — it was not measured before 01:34:26.

productcatalogservice logs were never actually read: the Loki selector used a hyphenated label value that does not match the service name, and the empty result is at least as consistent with a label mismatch as with silence (tr_df0b45ed3f5b). A re-query with the correct label is needed before any claim about what the service logged.

No frontend latency data was retrieved at all — both frontend metric dispatches returned only error ratios with no per-dependency breakdown and no quantiles (tr_926489735ab4, tr_b4f2d77fccb8). The frontend-side step at 01:34:26 is inferred from traces, not confirmed from metrics, so onset time and the size of user-visible impact are not independently established.

Whether the traffic-shaping attachment was an authorised chaos/fault-injection experiment or an erroneous automation action is unsettled; that determines whether the fix is to stop an experiment or to correct the automation. The change record names only the principal, not the intent (tr_a548b460d72d).

Triage crossed four unmeasured edges and the alert list spans 12 services; no dispatch covered checkoutservice, recommendationservice or loadgenerator directly, so I am attributing their alerts to the shared productcatalogservice path by trace inference only.
The change query covered a bounded window; whether any earlier change (before the queried interval) contributes to the ~900 ms flag tier was not checked.

configuration that made it fail lived somewhere else entirely, in a component with no
